newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan to give way in Islamist army row.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan to give way in Islamist army row.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan looked set to give ground at a cabinet meeting on Thursday to demands from the secularist army that he crack down on Islamist activism.
Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist leader, said he was willing to carry out some anti-Islamist measures wanted by the military.
"All requests will be taken into consideration. The ones that are in line with the constitution and the laws will be carried out," Anatolian news agency quoted him as saying on Wednesday night.
But he said civilian authorities did not have to bow to the military-dominated National Security Council (MGK), which ordered the crackdown in a lengthy statement late last month.
"The MGK is not above parliament and the cabinet," he said. Turkish ministers have traditionally rubber-stamped decisions by the influential council.
The cabinet was to discuss the proposed Islamist crackdown at a weekly meeting beginning at 1000 GMT.

Coalition partner Tansu Ciller, a pro-Western secularist, is expected to push the prime minister for wide implementation of the measures wanted by the army. These include enforcing a ban on Islamic dress and restricting religious education.
"There is not the slightest thing in the MGK statement that contradicts our views," Foreign Minister Ciller told Turkish television on Wednesday night.
"Secularism is a condition for democracy," said Ciller, head of the True Path Party (DYP).
Political analysts say Erbakan will probably give concessions on demands that he does not see as directly affecting his grassroots support.

Commentators say that without upsetting his Islamist voters he can bring illegal Koranic instruction under official control and license tens of thousands of shotguns that the army fears may be used by religious militants.

But Erbakan is unlikely to consent to the generals' demands that the coalition legislate against peaceful Islamist dissent and restrict the number of religious secondary schools, known as "Imam Hatips".
Many supporters of Erbakan's Welfare Party (RP) and some of his ministers were educated at religious shcools.

"Any compromise that ends with the closure of Imam Hatips and the abuse of human rights and freedoms will be a decree of death for the DYP and RP," columnist Fehmi Koru wrote in the Zaman daily, a moderate Islamist paper that often criticises Erbakan.
The secularist military has staged three coups since 1960.

The army's latest involvement in politics has strained the unity of the coalition, formed last June after months of bargaining and an interim government. Welfare won a narrow victory with 21 percent of the vote at general elections in 1995.
